history.heading: Dutch trading hub
paragraphs: Curaçao, an island off the coast of Venezuela, was home to the Caquetío people. The Spanish arrived in 1499, and the Dutch West India Company took the island in 1634, making Willemstad a major trading port.

Curaçao became one of the main centres of the Caribbean slave trade, through which enslaved Africans were sold to plantations across the region. In 1795 Tula led a major slave revolt. Slavery was abolished in 1863. Willemstad's synagogue, founded by Sephardic Jews in 1651, is the oldest in continuous use in the Americas.

history.heading: Oil and autonomy
paragraphs: A large Shell oil refinery opened in 1918 to process Venezuelan crude, bringing prosperity and migrants. Curaçao was the seat of government of the Netherlands Antilles from 1954. Labour riots on 30 May 1969 led to social and political change. When the Antilles were dissolved in 2010, Curaçao became a constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands.

culture.heading: Papiamentu and festivals
paragraphs: Papiamentu, a Creole language, is spoken by most people and is official alongside Dutch and English. The culture blends African, Dutch, Latin American and Sephardic influences.
Willemstad's colourful waterfront Handelskade is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Tambú music, carnival and the Curaçao liqueur, made from the peel of the local laraha orange, are well known.

politics.heading: Constituent country
paragraphs: Curaçao is a self-governing country within the Kingdom of the Netherlands, with its own parliament (Staten) and prime minister. The Dutch monarch is represented by a governor, and the kingdom handles defence and foreign affairs. Curaçaoans are Dutch citizens.

economy.heading: Tourism and services
paragraphs: Tourism, financial services, port activities and ship repair are the main sectors. The refinery, once the backbone of the economy, stopped operating in 2019. The currency is the Caribbean guilder, introduced in 2025 to replace the Netherlands Antillean guilder.
